abstract: To enhance learning and training, VR haptic devices must provide safe and physically accurate feedback that helps users build intuitions about force and motion. We present SafeForce, a method for rendering force feedback by capturing user input and reconfiguring a compliant mechanism in real time to align perceived with expected forces. We implemented SafeForce in a grounded Encountered-Type Haptic Display (ETHD) and demonstrated its versatility through three representative physics scenarios: pushing a stationary object, experiencing electrostatic repulsion, and bouncing a moving object. A user study with 29 participants showed that users adapted to new interaction profiles within 2-3 trials, and that rendered forces remained within perceptual thresholds except in the heaviest and most dynamic conditions. These results suggest that SafeForce enables rapid, perceptually aligned, and educationally valuable interactions with moving virtual objects.

abstract: Virtual reality (VR) applications face a critical trade-off: while visual immersion is the core experience, it often induces cybersickness (CS), leading to user attrition. Existing visual interventions (e.g., field-of-view restriction) alleviate discomfort at the cost of compromising immersion. Auditory interventions have been widely applied in mitigating motion sickness (MS), such as through music interventions and synchronized sound effects. Among all MS mitigation approaches, anticipatory audio cues have demonstrated effectiveness in vehicular MS contexts, reducing symptoms by approximately 17%. However, questions remain regarding VR cybersickness (CS): Do anticipatory audio cues remain effective in highly immersive virtual environments, where the dominance of visual interaction in VR may alter cue perception compared to that in MS contexts? How can VR motion intensity information be encoded, given that such information is largely absent in current mitigation strategies? How can anticipatory audio cues be systematically designed for CS mitigation through explicit mapping frameworks that link visual motion parameters to audio features? To address these gaps, this study establishes an optical flow mapping framework that encodes motion direction through stereo positioning and intensity through temporal patterns, delivering the results 2 seconds in advance. A within-subjects experiment (N = 24) was conducted in VR roller coaster environments, in which four conditions were compared. Results demonstrated a significant reduction in cybersickness across all audio conditions (direction-only: d = 0.862; intensity-only: d = 0.670; combined: d = 1.497, p < .001), with combined cues outperforming single-dimension alternatives (p < .016). All interventions preserved visual immersion (M ≈ 4.0/5) and maintained high usability metrics. This framework demonstrates that non-visual predictive cues can address the immersion-comfort trade-off in VR applications.

abstract: Virtual Reality offers highly immersive experiences, yet users remain physically situated in real-world environments whose layouts often differ from the virtual spaces they perceive. In these settings, users’ spatial memory of the physical environment may interact with or even conflict with the virtual scene, potentially influencing locomotion, task performance, and situational awareness. Despite its importance, the influence of physical space memory on VR interaction remains largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we conducted three controlled studies that varied the virtual scene and task structure to examine how physical-space memory affects VR performance. In Study I, participants interacted with virtual props placed at different distances from real obstacles, returning to a fixed start point after each trial to isolate the effect of obstacle proximity on immediate strategies. Study II used the same setup but removed the resets, allowing us to observe how memory reliance changes as task duration increases. In Study III, we introduced virtual anchors with varying degrees of alignment to physical landmarks, assessing how spatial similarity between the two spaces influences navigation and task efficiency. Our findings reveal that users subconsciously adapt their navigation and decision-making based on remembered surroundings, even when no visual cues are available. These insights deepen our understanding of spatial cognition in immersive VR and provide actionable guidelines for designing safer, more efficient, and cognitively consistent virtual environments.

abstract: Collaborative tasks in Virtual Reality, such as jointly manipulating objects, require tight multi-user synchronization. However, users often operate in heterogeneous physical environments with varying room sizes, furniture layouts, and obstacles. Enforcing a single, globally consistent virtual scene across such diversity constrains users’ natural movements, underutilizes available physical space, and ultimately degrades collaboration efficiency. We present CoVR, a novel framework that enables seamless multi-user collaboration in VR across heterogeneous physical spaces by prioritizing interaction alignment over strict spatial alignment. Instead of requiring all users to share an identical virtual scene, CoVR provides each user with a personalized virtual scene layout while maintaining synchronized actions and consistent collaborative outcomes. Technically, we formulate a multi-user coupled optimization problem that jointly optimizes per-user layouts to maximize usable space and facilitate seamless task execution. A key challenge arises from bi-directional dependencies: one user’s optimized layout determines feasible trajectories, which in turn constrain other users’ optimizations, and vice versa. To tackle this, CoVR introduces an iterative joint optimization algorithm alternating between personalized scene refinement and cross-user synchronization until convergence. We evaluate CoVR across typical collaborative tasks. Results show that CoVR significantly outperforms conventional scene alignment methods, leading to notable improvements in spatial efficiency, task completion time, and user comfort. These findings underscore its potential for scalable, natural, and efficient multi-user VR collaboration.

abstract: High-quality facial animation retargeting is crucial in digital entertainment production, enabling the transfer of animations from a source rig to a target rig. To avoid the need of manual transfer, automatic retargeting methods can be employed. However, creating universal methods remains challenging due to varying rig and topologies. We propose a novel retargeting method based on the idea that any facial expression can be decomposed into a weighted sum of Facial Action Coding System (FACS) poses. Our method assumes that these decompositions transfer across rigs with minimal need of refinement. We utilize a machine learning model to extract FACS weights from source frames. This model is trained solely on source animation data, requiring no target data or complex correspondence mappings. After a refinement step, these weights are then applied to the target rig’s FACS poses. Our technique supports seamless animation transfer across different rigs while allowing for artistic modifications by adjusting individual FACS poses. Our experiments demonstrate that this method produces high-quality retargeted animations and outperforms other retargeting methods. We explore how different design choices impact retargeting quality and showcase artistic control of asymmetries. By simplifying the workflow for rigged heads, this flexible framework enhances production efficiency while maintaining artistic control.

abstract: Over the past two decades, researchers have made significant steps in simulating agent-based human crowds, yet most efforts remain focused on low-level tasks such as collision avoidance, path following, and flocking. As a result, these approaches often struggle to capture the high-level behaviors that emerge from sustained agent-agent and agent-environment interactions over time. We introduce Generative LLM-Informed Modeling for Characters (GLIMC), a generative framework that produces crowd scenarios capturing agent–agent and agent–environment interactions, shaping coherent high-level crowd plans. To avoid the labor-intensive process of collecting and annotating real crowd video data, we leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) to bootstrap synthetic datasets of crowd scenarios. To represent those scenarios, we propose a time-expanded graph structure encoding actions, interactions, and spatial context. GLIMC employs a dual Variational Graph Autoencoder (VGAE) architecture that jointly learns connectivity patterns and node features conditioned on textual and structural signals, overcoming the limitations of direct LLM generation to enable scalable, environment-aware multi-agent crowd simulations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on scenarios with diverse behaviors such as, a University Campus and a Train Station, showing that it generates heterogeneous crowds, coherent interactions, and high-level decision-making patterns consistent with the provided context.

abstract: The generation of consistent multi-view images is essential for diffusion-based 3D texture synthesis, a key component of modern 3D content pipelines. However, existing methods remain weakly coupled across viewpoints, often exhibiting inconsistencies between views that result in artifacts such as ghosting, misalignment, and texture distortions. We introduce PixelSync, a training-free mechanism that explicitly enforces multi-view consistency during the diffusion process. Our method operates in two stages. First, we compute visibility-aware pixel correspondences between known views in a fast pre-computation step by utilizing geometric information obtained from a given 3D model. Then, during the diffusion process, we enforce consistency through two complementary algorithms: (i) attention synchronization, by modifying the attention scores in the U-Net’s down- and mid-blocks, and (ii) latent synchronization, by progressively aligning features on their corresponding shared pixels. PixelSync can be seamlessly integrated into pre-trained diffusion models without retraining, offering a lightweight and effective solution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach for generative texture synthesis by plugging PixelSync into established multi-view diffusion backbones, showcasing reduced cross-view artifacts and improved global coherence across standard quantitative and qualitative evaluations.

abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) are increasingly being used as tools to map coordinates to signals, encompassing applications from neural fields to texture compression, shape representations, and beyond. Most INR methods are based on using high-dimensional projections of the initial coordinates through encoders such as grid or positional encoding. Nevertheless, positional encoding is often insufficient and grids, as we show in this paper, require high resolution for being able to learn. In this paper, we demonstrate that positional encoding can be used not only as a high-dimensional embedding but also decomposed as a series of meaningful points. We propose the Positional Encoding Coordinate System, where we treat the projection of the original coordinate at each frequency as a point of interest. We describe the motion of each point with respect to the frequencies and show that it follows a unique pattern. Finally, we use the unique motion of each point as a basis decomposition for doing learned positional encoding using grids. We prove, using three competitive applications— image representation, texture compression, and signed distance function—that the proposed approach outperforms the current state of the art methods, and often requires 25% less parameters for equivalent reconstruction error or rendering.

abstract: 3D Aesthetics is significant in digital design, shaping how users experience real-time 3D content in games, VR, and product design. However, creating aesthetically pleasing shapes remains challenging due to diverse subjective standards and the lack of tools that support aesthetics-driven editing. Users often rely on intuition without explicit guidance on visual appeal, making aesthetic refinement slow, inconsistent, and cognitively demanding, particularly in fast-paced, iterative workflows. To address this challenge, we conducted in-depth interviews with design experts to identify challenges in aesthetics-oriented modeling workflows. Based on the findings, we developed Aesthetic3D, a 3D modeling interface offering real-time aesthetic scores learned from human perceptual data. Furthermore, Aesthetic3D seamlessly integrates the learned aesthetic measure into intuitive editing operations, enabling aesthetics-driven exploration and refinement of shape geometry. We evaluated Aesthetic3D through an ablation study, an open-ended study, and two generalization evaluations. Comprehensive experiments show that with Aesthetic3D, users can easily and effectively enhance the aesthetic appeal of 3D shapes.

abstract: Intrinsic decomposition — which expresses image colors as the product of diffuse albedo and shading, possibly augmented with view-dependent residuals — has a long history in image editing as it enables the modification of object colors and textures without altering lighting. We extend intrinsic decomposition to radiance fields represented with Gaussian splatting by proposing solutions to three key aspects of such decomposition. First, we describe how to model the intrinsic decomposition as independent sets of Gaussian primitives, which allows each set to adapt to the characteristics of the layer it represents. Second, we present an optimization procedure guided by data-driven predictions to disentangle multi-view photographs of a scene into the aforementioned intrinsic sets. Finally, we provide an editing workflow where users modify the texture of planar surfaces simply by modifying the albedo of that surface in one image. Capturing this edit within the intrinsic radiance field allows re-rendering of the edited scene with plausible lighting under arbitrary viewpoints.

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of unpaired shape translation on 3D point clouds. While prior methods typically rely on global latent vectors or spatially structured grids, such representations often lack the flexibility to capture both semantic structures and fine-grained geometric details. To address this, we propose operating directly in a structured token space, where tokens are pretrained through masked auto encoding. Unlike rigid spatial grids that impose fixed layouts, our tokens naturally adapt to geometric variations while maintaining semantic coherence. This structured yet flexible latent space enables semantically meaningful and geometrically precise transformations. A transformer-based translator is proposed to manipulate these tokens. This gated dual-branch translator enables detail-preserving and topology-aware shape translation across categories. Experiments on challenging tasks, such as chair-to-table transformations, demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in preserving both global structure and part-level details.

abstract: Algorithms leveraging ReSTIR-style spatiotemporal reuse have recently proliferated, hugely increasing effective sample count for light transport in real-time ray and path tracers. Many papers have been published on novel theoretical improvements, but algorithmic improvements and engineering insights toward optimal implementation have largely been neglected. We demonstrate enhancements to ReSTIR PT that make it 2–3x faster, decrease both visual and numerical error, and improve its robustness, making it closer to production-ready. We halve the spatial reuse cost by reciprocal neighbor selection, robustify shift mappings with new footprint-based reconnection criteria, and reduce spatiotemporal correlation with duplication maps. We further improve both performance and quality by extensive optimization, unifying direct and global illumination into the same reservoirs, and utilizing existing techniques for color noise and disocclusion noise reduction.

abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting is a popular representation for radiance field reconstruction, distinguished by the rendering speed of its rasterization-based renderer. While 3D Gaussians can also be raytraced, this approach has so far been slower, with 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing (3DGRT) taking nearly one order of magnitude longer to optimize. To address this, we present GRay, a fast ray tracer for 3D Gaussians designed to close this performance gap and match 3DGS's speed. Our method leverages the algorithmic difference between both approaches: unlike rasterization, ray tracing evaluates only Gaussians that are actually intersected by a ray, leading to potentially logarithmic—rather than linear—scaling in the number of primitives. This property allows ray tracing to better exploit dense scenes composed of numerous tiny Gaussians, a configuration which has largely been overlooked. Notably, we show that dense initialization—which creates many small primitives—slows down rasterization, but instead speeds up ray tracing. Designed to leverage this effect, GRay renders nearly 4× faster and optimizes nearly 10× faster than 3DGRT while maintaining similar quality, and has competitive speed with 3DGS albeit with somewhat lower quality. Code will be released upon publication.

abstract: Implicit surfaces offer distinct advantages over traditional boundary representations, including infinite resolution, low memory footprint, smooth geometry by construction, and support for non-destructive modeling. In this work, we introduce a method for localizing geometric detail in a way that preserves the mathematical properties required for accurate and efficient rendering using sphere tracing. Our contributions include novel procedural modeling techniques that expand the range of repetition patterns achievable in implicit surfaces; an interpolation-based approach that maintains field correctness while remaining computationally efficient; and a cache-based acceleration strategy that significantly improves the rendering performance of domain-repeated implicit geometries.

abstract: Frametime spikes and graphical fidelity both influence the feel of first-person shooter (FPS) games, yet their combined effects are not well understood. This paper examines how graphics settings and frametime spike magnitude interact with player performance and experience. We developed a custom FPS game with configurable textures, lighting, and visual effects, and induced frametime spikes of 0~ms, 225~ms, or 675~ms during play. Twenty-one participants completed all combinations while providing performance data and subjective ratings for visual quality and smoothness. Results show that graphical fidelity primarily affects perceived visual quality, while frametime spikes strongly reduce perceived smoothness. Performance (i.e., score and accuracy) declines with larger spikes but remains largely unchanged across graphics settings. These findings suggest that spike magnitude, rather than graphical fidelity, is the dominant factor shaping smoothness and performance, while players still notice and prefer higher-fidelity visuals.

abstract: In this paper, we rethink the controllable motion synthesis as a problem of manifold restriction rather than manifold construction. Based on this perspective, we propose a prior-first, condition-second framework for body-conditioned hand motion completion. Our framework first learns a generic body–hand kinematic prior from large-scale unstructured and unlabeled motion data, capturing the intrinsic coordination between global body dynamics and hand articulation. Semantic control is then introduced through lightweight adaptation on top of the frozen prior, avoiding the need to relearn kinematic structure for each control interface. At the core of our framework is a streaming, autoregressive body–hand prior that completes temporally coherent and kinematically consistent hand motion given global body motion. The prior is designed for online inference and real-time use, and incorporates structured kinematic modeling to maintain mechanical coupling between the body and the hands. To enable practical controllability under limited supervision, we introduce semantically-layered adapters that inject conditioning signals at appropriate kinematic levels, supporting both self-supervised attribute control and weakly supervised text-driven control with only a few hours of labeled data. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our framework improves kinematic plausibility, robustness, and controllability compared to end-to-end conditioned baselines, particularly in low-resource and cross-dataset settings. We further showcase real-time inference and an interactive authoring workflow, highlighting the applicability to production animation pipelines.

abstract: In computer graphics and engineering, isotropic hyperelastic volumetric materials are commonly chosen from a small set of families (e.g., StVK, linear corotational, Neo-Hookean, Ogden) and tuned by adjusting family-specific parameters. This workflow obscures how different material families relate and provides no unified notion of “distance” or “amount and direction of nonlinearity” across families. Furthermore, for a general isotropic 3D hyperelastic energy density function y; the relationships between its parameter values, and visually intuitive properties such as an object’s “stiffness”, volume preservation, or the “amount of nonlinearity”, are less clear and can be tedious to adjust. Starting with an arbitrary isotropic y; we define and compute Lamé parameters (capturing linear behavior: stiffness and volume preservation), using the Taylor expansion of y at the rest state. This makes it possible to quantitatively “equalize” the small-deformation behavior of two materials, even if they come from different material families, or are defined by arbitrary isotropic energy densities y: We rigorously state and prove that Linear Corotational materials (arguably the most widely used materials in computer graphics) are the simplest possible nonlinear materials. To compare nonlinear behavior beyond the linearization, we define a distance metric between linearization-matched materials, using third-order terms of y (“weakly nonlinear behavior”). We further define SCIEN, a directional nonlinearity measure obtained by projecting a material onto the standard one-parameter Seth-Hill continuum (which includes Hencky, Linear Corotational, and StVK as special cases), thereby distinguishing stretch-stiffening from compressionstiffening and quantifying its strength. As a result, we can equalize and edit materials agnostically from any material family: two materials can be matched in small-deformation response, in weakly nonlinear behavior, or in both, while keeping these properties decoupled. This provides a unified language and practical tools for comparing, organizing, and adjusting common nonlinear material models.

abstract: Music-driven character animation enables and enhances transformative applications in entertainment and interactive education. However, synthesizing realistic drumming motion from audio remains challenging due to the inherent tension between high-acceleration dynamics and the need for extreme spatial-temporal precision. Existing approaches, often reliant on motion matching or MIDI input, struggle with generalizing to diverse real-world audio. Moreover, the field lacks standardized evaluation metrics capable of distinguishing precise drumming from noisy motion. In this paper, we introduce a generative diffusion framework featuring a dual-objective loss function that decouples skeletal integrity from drumstick precision, thus enabling centimeter-level stick precision without sacrificing natural body dynamics. Additionally, leveraging our own dataset and data augmentation strategy, the model generalizes to non-curated, in-the-wild audio. To rigorously evaluate performance, we propose two novel metrics: an impact-to-target distance to quantify spatial precision and an audio-motion correlation score to assess temporal alignment. Our quantitative analysis and user studies demonstrate that our system generates high-quality motion that is often indistinguishable from ground-truth performances.

abstract: Reconstructions of surgical scenes from endoscopic video are useful for surgical training and medical animation, as they accurately capture the clinician’s viewpoint. In practice, however, 3D scenes acquired through endoscopy, increasingly represented as 3D Gaussian splats (3DGS), are typically constrained to limited viewpoint ranges. Consequently, even small endoscope camera motions can significantly degrade rendering fidelity and organ shape reconstruction. This gap prevents the direct use of such scenes in physics-based surgical simulation, which requires accurate, shape-consistent geometry. To address this, we propose a pipeline that combines the visual realism of an endoscopic 3DGS scene with simulation-ready organ geometry extracted from pre-operative 3D computed tomography (CT) or MRI scans. Because the pre-operative and endoscopically observed organs often differ in pose, deformation, and geometric completeness, we register the full segmented anatomy onto its partial corresponding region in the splat representation using a mesh-free, elastically regularized alignment method. We perform this alignment in the reduced-order deformation space of Simplicits, an existing state-of-the-art mesh-free simulator based on learned skinning weights, which has not previously been applied to surgical endoscope-captured organs because no CT-grounded alignment pipeline existed to bridge the two modalities. Using its reduced basis, we optimize on the order of 10–20 handle transforms rather than thousands of tetrahedral-mesh vertices. We employ a two-stage procedure: (1) a weighted rigid iterative closest point (ICP), (2) followed by a reduced-order elastic ICP, with a Neo-Hookean elastic energy term and a geometry matching term that uses nearest-neighbour correspondences to the 3DGS target. As shown in Figure 1, our pipeline produces CT-grounded, physics-simulatable organ assets that are visually aligned with the hyper-realistic tissue surfaces captured by endoscopic 3DGS reconstructions, closing the gap between photoreal scene capture and simulation-ready geometry.

abstract: Traditional garment simulation for animated characters is a time-consuming bottleneck for artists due to slow simulations and tedious parameter tunings. Recent data-driven methods offer a powerful alternative, capable of learning from a dataset of simulated data to generate high-quality deformations. A lightweight network design allows data-driven systems to achieve a real-time inference speed. This significantly improves the artist workflow, as they can interactively pose a character and see high-quality folds and wrinkles at animation time, thereby allowing to make creative decisions ahead of time. However, existing neural clothing methods have presented appealing results on datasets based on realistic human models (e.g., SMPL), but when trained on animated character datasets, they struggle to generalize to unseen poses. In this paper, we aim at designing neural networks and training strategies to generalize better to unseen poses in real-time to enable the interactive posing applications. We focus on a production-oriented setting where the model is trained for a single garment in a quasi-static setup. Technically, we leverage a smooth, expressive latent space by first training a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE). We then progressively train the VAE encoder to transition from reconstruction to pose-driven prediction. To guide this prediction, we condition the network on both low-dimensional pose parameters and character body surface displacements. Finally, we introduce a novel local gradient histogram loss that mitigates the over-smoothing effect of reconstruction losses. Extensive evaluations on production-level assets and public datasets demonstrate that our method produces sharp, realistic wrinkles, smooth large-scale drape, and temporal coherence in real-time, offering a robust and easily integrable solution for interactive posing workflows.

abstract: Speech-driven 3D facial animation plays a pivotal role in immersive digital human applications. Recent works have explored Mamba-based sequence modeling as an efficient alternative to Transformer, but they often suffer from limited cross-modal alignment and insufficient control over fine-grained facial deformations. To address these limitations, we propose FaceMamba framework. First, we introduce a Multi-Granularity Audio Encoder (MG-AE) to provide richer conditioning for motion synthesis. Second, we propose a Gated-Cross Mamba Decoder (GC-MD), which performs dynamic modulation of audio features within the state-space modeling process, significantly improving audio-visual alignment while retaining near-linear complexity. We further design a 3D structural consistency loss (Lstruct ) that explicitly enforces anatomically plausible facial deformations in mesh space. In addition, we introduce a geometry-aware evaluation metric to quantitatively assess the structural fidelity of generated 3D facial sequences. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FaceMamba outperforms state-of-the-art methods, improving the MVE and ESE metrics by 2.3% and 2.9% on BIWI, and by 2.8% and 4.0% on Vocaset, respectively. Notably, for a 20-second sequence, our framework keeps the inference time under 0.25s, which is 1.6x faster than the SOTA. Our work provides new insights into geometry-aware audio-driven facial synthesis.

abstract: Garment animation systems are essential for high-fidelity digital characters in various applications such as films and video games. We propose SSILK, a neural network-based method that is explicitly designed to handle loose garments such as capes and robes, garment types that are notoriously hard to simulate via pose-based garment neural simulators. We achieve this through three contributions. First, we formulate our method as a latent-space time integration scheme inspired by Verlet integration, resulting in more temporally stable garment dynamics compared to prior methods. Second, we employ a hybrid proxy-joint and blendshape decoder to represent full SO(3) transformations that can be too challenging to capture using blendshapes alone. Finally, we propose a data-augmentation strategy to improve performance on out-of-distribution scenarios. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on various garment and character animations and compare it to the state of the art.

abstract: Realistic animal motion for virtual production is typically obtained either through motion capture of highly trained performers who accurately mimic animal behavior, or by retargeting ordinary human motion using complex control setups. Both approaches are challenging and often fail to fully reproduce the nuances of natural animal motion, motivating data-driven alternatives. We present an automatic human-to-quadruped puppeteering framework that produces plausible and controllable quadruped motions from ordinary human motion data. Our approach employs a two-stage generative diffusion model trained purely on quadruped motion data. By introducing a structured conditioning and inpainting strategy, our method supports a wide range of actions, including walking, running, jumping, sitting, and lying. Furthermore, we enable fine-grained intuitive control of the quadruped motion such as head movement control and individual limb puppeteering. Experimental results demonstrate improved motion realism and controllability compared to existing retargeting approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of our framework as a tool for animation and virtual production applications.

abstract: Motion editing is central to VFX and game development, where it is used extensively to modify and augment existing movements to conform to new environments or changes in artistic direction. While traditional motion editing can do small modifications, it cannot accommodate larger structural edits, resulting in visual warping artifacts that require authoring new motion. Conversely, recent advances in large-scale generative modeling have unlocked newfound capabilities for authoring entire movements by directly manipulating sparse spatial constraints. While impressive at creating new movements, these methods lack the capability to preserve and edit existing motion interactively. In this work, we introduce scheduled inpainting, a method that enables interactive generative motion editing, a novel paradigm unifying motion synthesis and editing by leveraging generative models. Scheduled inpainting is a simple yet powerful inference-based technique that enables fine-grained spatiotemporal control over the balance between preserving the original motion and generating new content. By building atop generative models that support direct manipulation, our system allows artists to interactively refine existing animations while ensuring results remain natural and consistent with the learned motion distribution. Scheduled inpainting is versatile and supports many editing applications, such as extending, stitching, and compositing different clips. Finally, we extensively validate our approach by comparing with four baselines, conducting ablations of our design, and reporting user feedback.

abstract: Speech-driven 3D facial animation has achieved remarkable realism, yet existing models suffer from severe performance degradation on unseen languages due to discrepancies in articulation patterns and motion distributions. We attribute this limitation to a distribution shift on the latent motion manifold, where pretrained vector-quantized (VQ) codebooks fail to adequately cover target-language articulation regions. To address this, we propose Manifold-Aligned VQ Convolutional Adapters for parameter-efficient cross-lingual adaptation. abstract: Abstract Data sparsity is a central challenge in pervasive computing and human–machine interactive systems, where observations arise unevenly across users, devices, algorithms, and environments. Across recommender interfaces, healthcare monitoring, smart-city mobility, and language-enabled interaction, sparsity can reflect incomplete sensing, constrained exposure, intermittent participation, privacy limits, and heterogeneous event generation. These mechanisms can produce missing or weakly supported instances as well as observable structures such as excess zeros and long-tail frequency distributions; conflating mechanisms with their manifestations can lead to mismatched modelling and evaluation. This survey synthesises 134 studies and develops a source-to-structure diagnostic framework. It distinguishes two mechanism-oriented perspectives—data collection oriented sparsity and user–system interaction oriented sparsity—from a distributional structure oriented perspective that records observable zero-inflated and long-tail patterns without assuming their causes. Six operational forms are connected through a support-based chain from mechanism to observational support, observable structure, and intervention. The roadmap further distinguishes evidence acquisition, bias correction, robust learning under fixed sparsity, and decentralised utilisation, and specifies cross-domain transfer conditions, mechanism- and structure-aware evaluation, and human-centred trade-offs for conditional method selection.

abstract: Abstract Georeferenced time series are central to domains such as urban planning and climate studies, yet insights remain difficult to obtain when patterns span multiple variables and scales. Analysts often seek events —abrupt changes that may co‐occur across variables, space, and time. The Graph Wavelet Transform (GWT) is effective for detecting such changes; however, previous visualization tools have primarily applied it to univariate signals. We introduce ManyWaves , a visual analytics system that applies GWT separately to each variable and integrates the resulting event information in a coordinated multivariate environment. Each variable is modelled as a signal on a shared spatiotemporal graph, and its high‐frequency wavelet coefficients characterize local spatial and temporal changes. A 1D convolutional autoencoder then learns a low‐dimensional representation from these coefficients, which drives linked views: a projection of locations by event similarity, a heatmap summarizing when variables change, and spatial and time‐series views for detailed inspection. Through three case studies—U.S. flight disruptions, traffic and crime in São Paulo, and land‐use change in the Brazilian Legal Amazon—we show how ManyWaves supports the exploration of multivariate events. Expert feedback suggests that the system's event‐oriented views and interactions support sense‐making, while also highlighting the need for onboarding to interpret wavelet‐based representations.

abstract: Abstract The proliferation of highly realistic forged images, driven by advances in generative models such as GANs and diffusion models, poses serious challenges to information security and digital forensics. While existing detection methods leveraging spatial-domain features have shown progress, they often struggle to generalize to ever-evolving forgery techniques–particularly AI-generated content. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Multi-scale Fourier Enhancement Network that integrates frequency-domain analysis with multi-scale feature learning. Our approach incorporates a lightweight Fourier Enhancement Module into a ConvNeXt backbone, enabling the capture of frequency anomalies introduced by forgery operations. Combined with a multi-scale fusion mechanism and a hybrid loss function, the model achieves robust feature learning from local textures to global semantics. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves superior accuracy and robustness while maintaining computational efficiency, and shows promising cross-generator generalization performance on unseen generative sources.

abstract: The problem of covering a two-dimensional region with identical circles of minimal radius (CRICMR) is a classic optimization problem with many relevant real-world applications. However, due to the nonconvexity and the multiply-connected nature of the region to be covered, designing an efficient formulation and solution approach for the problem is very challenging. In this study, we first propose a unified optimization model for two classic variants of the problem (i.e., the CRICMR problems with and without center placement constraints), and then present an effective heuristic algorithm for solving both variants. The proposed model is based on the clipped Voronoi diagram and converts the intractable region coverage problem into the much easier vertex covering problem with respect to the clipped Voronoi polygons. The proposed algorithm incorporates several key components: a two-phase monotonic basin-hopping method; a subregion-based local optimization method; two perturbation operators, and a radius adjustment method for the covering circles. Computational experiments on popular benchmark instances demonstrate the efficiency of our approach, which significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods by improving the current best-known solutions for nearly all benchmark instances. abstract: In this work, we propose a preconditioned augmented Lagrangian method (ALM) for solving semidefinite programming (SDP) problems. The preconditioner is implemented via a weighted penalty function in the ALM subproblem, with the weight matrix derived from the projection operator onto the tangent space of the feasible region. This simple yet effective modification significantly accelerates ALM, particularly for ill-conditioned SDPs. By combining the preconditioned ALM with our previously developed feasible method, SDPF, we develop SDPF+, an SDP solver capable of handling convex problems with possibly nonlinear objective functions. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the efficiency and robustness of SDPF+, showing that it can generally outperform other solvers on large-scale SDPs whose optimal solutions exhibit low-rank structure. abstract: We study the optimal pricing problem for operations at a seaport terminal within a multimodal transport network, where the terminal operator sets differentiated prices for processing cargoes arriving via and transferred to various modes of transport. The problem incorporates two critical features: (i) the influence of port congestion on cargo suppliers’ terminal selection and (ii) the hierarchical choice structure that predicts how cargo suppliers select transport modes and routes for their cargoes. To capture these features, we formulate the problem as a nonconvex, nonlinear program involving a nested logit choice model and an equilibrium constraint reflecting the congestion effect, which is challenging to solve or analyze. To address this difficulty, we apply a change of variables to reformulate the price-based model as a flow-based model, where cargo flows, rather than prices, are the decision variables, thereby making the model more amenable to analysis. By exploiting the structure of the flow-based model, we derive an optimality equation whose dimension scales only with the number of origin-destination (O/D) pairs, which effectively reduces the computational complexity by avoiding directly handling the numerous variables associated with transport routes. This approach not only applies to seaport revenue management problems that often involve multiple transport modes and a substantial number of routes, but also contributes a structure-exploiting method for addressing a broader class of nonlinear programs involving equilibrium constraints and customer choice models. We show that, for each O/D pair, the optimal mode-dependent prices decompose into a component common across modes plus a mode-specific adjustment. We also establish analytical bounds on the revenue loss induced by misspecifying cargo suppliers’ choice structure. We evaluate the performance of the algorithm by comparing it with several widely used benchmark methods through numerical analysis. Our findings indicate that our algorithm outperforms the benchmark methods in both revenue maximization and runtime. Moreover, we find that accurately modeling the choice structure has a larger impact on revenue than explicitly modeling congestion. abstract: Extensive simulation studies of reinforcement learning algorithms in pricing environments suggest that it may be possible for them to learn to collude when including a memory of one period. Theoretical analyses of this phenomenon have focused on the setting with two prices, while the simulations have been carried out with up to fifteen prices. Here, we address this gap by analyzing the probability of observing collusion by Decentralized Q-learning in a pricing duopoly with three possible prices and a memory of one period. Using the logit demand model for the payoffs leads to a payoff structure that is a three-action generalization of the iterated PD. Our central question is whether the addition of an intermediate action (or price) between “defection” and “cooperation” increases the likelihood of observing cooperation/collusion. The Decentralized Q-learning algorithm is provably convergent in this environment, and the basins of attraction of its equilibria can be calculated explicitly using Individual Best-Response Graphs. We find that even though the additional action increases the number of collusive equilibria, the likelihood of collusion does not increase. In addition, we find common structure in the possible strategy equilibria, identify conditions for their existence, and refine the notion of collusive strategy equilibria. Finally, we show that introducing fluctuations to the learning process drastically increases the likelihood of collusion, but not to the levels observed when introducing fluctuations in the environment with two prices. Designing effective antitrust policy and detection tools against the threat of algorithmic collusion requires understanding the mechanisms by which algorithms learn to collude. To this end, our results provide new insight into the drivers of collusion among reinforcement learners.

abstract: Abstract The Molecular Distance Geometry Problem is essential to structural biology, as it seeks to determine three-dimensional protein structures from partial interatomic distances. Its discretizable subclass (DMDGP) admits an exact combinatorial formulation that enables efficient exploration of the search space. However, in practical settings such as Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, distances are available only within uncertainty bounds, leading to the interval variant ( i DMDGP). We propose a hybrid combinatorial–continuous framework for solving the i DMDGP. The method combines an enumeration process derived from the DMDGP with a continuous refinement stage that minimizes a nonconvex stress function penalizing deviations from admissible distance intervals. This integration supports a systematic exploration guided by discrete structure and local optimization. The formulation incorporates torsion angle intervals and chirality constraints through an atom ordering that preserves protein-backbone geometry. Numerical experiments show that the approach efficiently reconstructs geometrically valid conformations even under wide distance bounds, whereas most existing studies assume narrow ones.

abstract: ABSTRACT Solutions and business architects play a fundamental role in the process of selecting software solutions that satisfy their organizations' objectives and needs to implement a change. These practitioners are often faced with the challenge of selecting the most suitable software among a set of candidate solutions. For that, they often perform a comparative study based on a set of criteria to select the software that best meets the specific needs of their organizations and customers. The software selection is a decision process that plays a crucial role in organizations' digital transformation. However, existing methods have limitations related to their usability and implementation complexity. This paper provides architecture practitioners with a novel method that automatically prioritizes software solutions in order to select the most suitable one. The prioritization process of the solutions is based on: (i) the functional requirements they implement and (ii) the desired goals (business objectives and non‐functional requirements) they satisfy. The proposed method is goal‐oriented. It uses the Goal‐oriented Requirement Language (GRL) that links the candidate software to the requirements to be implemented and the goals to be met. The use of GRL allows the method to automatically compute satisfaction scores that measure the effectiveness of candidate software solutions in implementing requirements and satisfying the desired goals. The satisfaction score is used to rank the software solutions. An experimental study was conducted to evaluate the method's usability. Results demonstrated its effectiveness and alignment with expert expectations in solutions, business architecture, and business analysis.

abstract: ABSTRACT One of the effects of COVID‐19 was that software engineers were forced to work remotely, in many cases without prior experience, which may have led to a number of challenges for projects and organizations, along with developers' well‐being. Several work styles were considered after the pandemic, because not only did teleworking persist but new forms of work emerged, for which neither organizations nor employees were prepared. These new modalities have led to challenges that have not yet been sufficiently addressed in the existing literature, mainly because they are relatively recent phenomena. The aim of this paper is to analyze the risks that remote or hybrid working can pose to software development and examine them from the perspective of the company, the project itself, and employees. Once the problems have been identified, it is important to analyze them from the point of view of a software engineer's personality and assess the likelihood of these challenges arising according to the working model used. It is also essential to find strategies with which to mitigate these challenges. These are the objectives of this paper, which aims to help project managers and developers carry out hybrid or remote software development efficiently and ensure their employees' well‐being. To achieve these objectives, a mixed‐methods approach comprising five stages was adopted: a systematic mapping review to identify and categorize the factors affecting software engineers, a survey of 184 practitioners to validate and refine these factors, a second survey examining the perceived impact of different work modalities on productivity and associated risks, and an evaluation of our framework (main contribution of this paper) through semi‐structured interviews with 10 practitioners.

abstract: Abstract Within the legal domain, named entity recognition (NER) is an essential pre-processing tool for important tasks such as information extraction and redaction. Research to date has focused on rule-based approaches or machine learning strategies that require significant time and effort to train through labelled corpora. Large, multi-purpose generative large language models (LLMs) have been successfully employed on natural language processing (NLP) tasks with no prior supervised training and may represent a way forward in addressing these existing bottlenecks. Despite promising results in certain NLP use cases, the Few-Shot LLM performance on unfamiliar, domain-specific NER tasks has, to date, remained uncertain. In this legal clause NER task, we evaluate a Few-Shot, Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting strategy for OpenAI’s GPT-4 LLM on a new CUAD-NER dataset that we have repurposed for the task of Person and Organisation entity identification. In a comparative study, we demonstrate that the GPT4 + Few-Shot CoT prompt strategy outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, achieving a 5% percentage point improvement in Micro F1 score over the best performing BERT base (cased) competitor. This study also takes the novel approach of assessing the business feasibility of deploying each of these machine learning models through a detailed cost–benefit analysis that measures the trade-off between performance metrics and low and high usage running costs.

abstract: Abstract Digital asset markets are expanding but remain difficult to evaluate, particularly for retail investors who face information overload, unstructured disclosures, and limited regulatory safeguards. Traditional due diligence methods often fail to capture the complexity of blockchain-based projects, exposing investors to misrepresentation and fraud. At the same time, LLMs have shown remarkable results on analyzing large information quantities. Thus, this paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can enhance digital asset assessments by providing inspectable, automated, and low-cost decision support. Using a Design Science Research methodology, we developed a framework and a prototype tool to apply LLM-based evaluation to token-offering whitepapers, evaluated across 1,139 generated runs covering 29 token offerings. We compared different content processing approaches, from raw document analysis to aspect-focused summarization, and tested prompting strategies including Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and Chain-of-Thought reasoning. Our findings show a nuanced pattern. On aggregate quantitative metrics, structured summarization combined with Chain-of-Thought prompting achieves the lowest rating error, although differences in rank correlation between configurations are not statistically resolvable given the number of projects evaluated; aspect-focused summarization structures criterion-specific evidence and candidate red flags explicitly, but its rating error is higher and the interpretability of this representation was not independently evaluated. To address the single-model limitation, we added a lightweight multi-model robustness check using two small open-source models on a matched subset of cases; the results suggest that the observed optimism bias is not specific to the original closed LLM, although performance still varies across model configurations. Overall agreement between model and expert ratings remains limited, which suggests that LLMs are better understood as decision-support tools for screening and explanation than as substitutes for expert judgment. The study therefore contributes a design-oriented due diligence artifact and a dependence-aware evaluation of how summarization and prompting choices affect calibration, output-level inspectability, and validity boundaries in digital asset assessment.

abstract: Abstract We give a new formulation of Turing reducibility in terms of higher modalities, inspired by an embedding of the Turing degrees in the lattice of subtoposes of the effective topos discovered by Hyland. In this definition, higher modalities play a similar role to I/O monads or dialogue trees in allowing a function to receive input from an external oracle. However, in homotopy type theory (HoTT), they have better logical properties than monads: they are compatible with higher types, and each modality corresponds to a reflective subuniverse that under suitable conditions is itself a model of HoTT. We give synthetic proofs of some basic results about Turing reducibility in cubical type theory making use of two axioms of Markov induction and computable choice . Both axioms are variants of axioms already studied in the effective topos. We show they hold in certain reflective subuniverses of cubical assemblies, demonstrate their use in some simple proofs in synthetic computability theory using modalities and show they are downwards absolute for oracle modalities. These results have been formalised using cubical mode of the Agda proof assistant. We explore some first connections between Turing reducibility and homotopy theory. This includes a synthetic proof that two Turing degrees are equal as soon as they induce isomorphic permutation groups on the natural numbers, making essential use of both Markov induction and the formulation of groups in HoTT as pointed, connected, 1-truncated types. We also give some simple non-topological examples of modalities in cubical assemblies based on these ideas, to illustrate what we expect higher-dimensional analogues of the Turing degrees to look like.

abstract: Abstract Despite their success, Deep Learning (DL) models are susceptible to spurious correlations. These are accidental correlations between non-predictive features of the training dataset and the target label, leading to models that do not generalise well to samples without such spurious correlations. We propose to address this failure mode by extending and improving an existing method for spurious correlation robustness — UnLearning from Experience (ULE). ULE trains two models in parallel; a biased model is encouraged to learn the spurious correlations, while a separate debiased model is trained to solve the same task while avoiding learning the same behaviour as the first, thus avoiding learning the spurious correlations. A weakness of ULE is that it treats every training example identically, regardless of whether or not it contains a spurious correlation. Therefore, ULE does not make optimal use of the training data, leading to worse-than-necessary performance. To address this weakness, we introduce Weighted UnLearning from Experience (wULE), which modifies the original ULE loss function to reweight the components depending on whether a training sample likely contains spurious correlations. Hence, we explore two methods for identifying training samples likely to contain spurious correlations. We test our approach using several well-known spurious correlation robustness benchmarks — Waterbirds, CelebA, UrbanCars and MultiNLI. Our novel wULE method outperforms the original ULE in all cases and achieves Worst-Group Accuracy (WGA) results comparable to the best methods in the spurious correlation robustness literature.

abstract: Abstract Data constraints are important business rules that specify the values allowed or required for the data used in a software system. These constraints are typically described in textual software artifacts ( e.g., requirements, developer documents, user manuals, etc. ). In this paper, we focus on automating the task of identifying data constraints in natural language software documents. In order to automate this task, we first study how data constraints are described in natural language. Specifically, we studied 546 data constraints described in the natural language artifacts of nine software systems. We uncovered and documented nine linguistic discourse patterns that stakeholders use to describe data constraints in natural language. We cast the constraint identification and extraction as a text matching and classification problem. We explore the suitability of traditional machine learning techniques, using the discourse patterns we discovered, together with other linguistic elements, as features, for automatically classifying sentence fragments as data constraint descriptions. The best combination of features and learner achieves 63.63% precision and 61.40% recall (62.34% F1). Automating the extraction of data constraints from natural language text is essential for automating their traceability to code, test generation, compliance analysis, etc.

abstract: ABSTRACT Modern cloud infrastructures must deliver energy‐efficient, high‐performance services while meeting Quality of Service (QoS) guarantees. However, dynamic workloads and heterogeneous hardware often create resource imbalances across hosts, triggering unnecessary virtual machine (VM) migrations, wasting energy, and increasing Service Level Agreement (SLA) violations. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an Energy‐Convergent migration framework for Dynamic VM Consolidation (DVMC) that integrates the Estimated Imbalance Degree (EID) with a probabilistic SLA Violation Detection Scheme (SDS). Our approach prioritizes migration using VM categorization with weight‐based criticality assessment. It employs mathematical models for demand estimation, Markov‐based load redistribution, bottleneck detection, forecasting, and energy‐aware migration planning. Formal theoretical analysis establishes the correctness of the framework, while efficient algorithms enable practical deployment under diverse cloud workloads. The proposed method accurately identifies host‐level imbalances and suppresses transient migrations through a unified threshold‐driven strategy. This approach enhances system stability and resource utilization. Experiments on OpenStack and CloudSim demonstrate average reductions of up to in energy consumption, in SLA violations, and in migrations compared with state‐of‐the‐art baselines, with the differences confirmed statistically at . Statistical and sensitivity analyses further confirm robustness and practical applicability.

abstract: ABSTRACT Context Pull requests play a pivotal role in the software development life‐cycle, and they produce an abundance of metrics about how contributors and reviewers make decisions within the pull‐based development model. Previous authors make analyses at the individual pull request level, which faces many challenging issues with the scarcity and noisiness of input data, and which yields signals that are difficult to compare between repositories. Objective This study investigates whether signals measured at the repository level characterize developer behavior more robustly than per‐pull‐request measures, and whether such signals generalize across hosting platforms and development contexts. We target two behaviors in particular: how review time responds to code complexity, and how concentrated reviewing is between pairs of developers. Methods We compare four sources of pull request data: Atlassian Bitbucket and Atlassian GitHub repositories from Atlassian Corporation Plc, both publicly available, and the Avatar and ISM/VET Bitbucket project repositories from J.P. Morgan. We first use an augmented Gaussian Mixture Model to model review time against code complexity, bucketed by meaningful lines of code. We then use a graph‐theoretical construction of authors and reviewers to analyze reviewer selection behavior between pairs of developers, from which we construct an aggregate index of overly co‐reviewing behavior and track it over a rolling window across a period of two years. Results Our mixture models fit the data well, and we leverage them to explore and explain instances where code complexity increases, but review time does not. Our index helps in identifying periods of high co‐reviewership, and recovers known episodes in the J.P. Morgan repositories in which single‐reviewer approval of large pull requests was expected. Conclusion Repository‐level signals sidestep the data scarcity and noise that constrain analyses at the individual pull request level, and they yield measures that can be compared across repositories. The inclusion of a public, open‐source GitHub dataset alongside closed‐source Bitbucket projects demonstrates that the methodology generalizes across platforms and development contexts.

abstract: ABSTRACT Background The deployment of soft sensors, data‐based models that estimate unobservable or costly variables from available sensor data, remains limited in IoT infrastructures by the resource constraints of IoT devices and the complexity of managing model lifecycles at scale. Objective This work presents a novel architecture that enables the end‐to‐end transformation, distribution and execution of soft sensors on IoT embedded devices. Methods The proposed approach leverages Kafka‐ML, a framework for managing ML models and data streams, which has been extended to orchestrate the end‐to‐end lifecycle of soft sensors in real time via IoT data streams. By enabling local inference on IoT devices, the system reduces reliance on cloud connectivity during operation: while initial deployment, model updates, and lifecycle orchestration via Kafka‐ML require network access, local inference allows the estimation of complex variables even when subsequent connectivity is unreliable or intermittent. The approach has been evaluated in two representative scenarios, non‐intrusive load monitoring (NILM) and water quality monitoring, each with different demands regarding communications overhead and accuracy. Results The automated quantization pipeline yields negligible accuracy degradation for the NILM scenario (MAE shifted from 2.836 to 2.837) and an acceptable performance trade‐off for water quality monitoring (MAE rose from 0.53 to 0.82 mg/L), while reducing inference latency by up to 4.6× compared to remote inference. Conclusions These results demonstrate the framework's capability to automate the deployment of distributed, autonomous, and privacy‐preserving soft sensors across heterogeneous monitoring scenarios.

abstract: Serverless workflows are commonly modeled as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) composed of fine-grained functions. While this design promotes modularity and programming flexibility, it also incurs frequent inter-function communication. To alleviate this performance overhead, function fusion has been explored to co-locate and execute communicating functions within a shared container instance. However, existing approaches fail to account for the time-varying trade-off between communication latency reduction and resource overprovisioning arising from path uncertainty in dynamic serverless workflows, making it difficult to sustain high resource efficiency over time. In this paper, we propose a new adaptive function fusion strategy that dynamically reconstructs serverless workflows by adjusting communication schemes between functions in response to changing workflow invocations. Realizing this strategy, however, requires jointly optimizing function fusion and per-instance configuration, a problem with a combinatorial search space, while managing the substantial overhead of switching fusion schemes at runtime. To address these challenges, we design AdaFuse, a novel system for dynamic serverless workflows. AdaFuse jointly optimizes function fusion and instance reconfiguration through an efficient beam-search–based algorithm to optimize the end-to-end resource allocation. With the optimized fusion scheme, AdaFuse employs a fluid migration mechanism that incrementally transitions the workflow deployment while seamlessly redirecting incoming workloads. Evaluations across diverse benchmarks show that AdaFuse reduces resource allocation by up to 49.4% compared to baselines, without compromising SLO attainment.

abstract: Cloud data centers increasingly rely on device virtualization to share high-bandwidth network adapters and accelerators among virtual machines (VMs). Single Root I/O Virtualization (SR-IOV) exposes Virtual Functions (VFs) directly to guest VMs, but the Input/Output Memory Management Unit (IOMMU) on the host processor becomes a bottleneck as the number of VFs grows: its small translation lookaside buffer (TLB) causes severe throughput degradation. Meanwhile, because the hypervisor cannot determine which guest memory regions are used for Direct Memory Access (DMA), it must pin the entire VM memory, preventing memory overcommitment and wasting physical resources. Existing solutions, including Address Translation Services (ATS), the Page Request Interface (PRI), and software-emulated virtual IOMMUs, suffer from compatibility, deployment, or CPU overhead limitations. We propose DMMU, a Device MMU system implemented on programmable SmartNICs that addresses both the IOMMU translation bottleneck and the memory-pinning barrier to overcommitment, with minimal host software modification and zero guest awareness. DMMU introduces two techniques: combo-DMA , which dynamically routes address translations between the IOMMU and an on-device translation engine depending on IOMMU load, and direct-PRI , which enables the SmartNIC to issue page fault requests directly to a host-side driver, bypassing the multi-layer emulation path of conventional PRI in virtualized environments. We implement DMMU through a microcode update to a commodity dual-port 100G NIC and evaluate it on Intel Skylake and Ice Lake servers. With a representative 120-VF configuration, DMMU improves NIC throughput by 65% and reduces IOTLB misses by 38 × compared to the baseline IOMMU. DMMU also enables reliable memory overcommitment with device passthrough, achieving near-baseline Redis performance at a 1.35 × overcommitment ratio.

abstract: Singular value decomposition (SVD) is a fundamental matrix factorization in scientific computing and data analysis, but computing it efficiently on modern GPUs remains challenging. Full SVD provides strong numerical robustness but is often expensive for large matrices, whereas randomized SVD (RSVD) improves performance but may exhibit accuracy variability, especially when the target rank is unknown or the singular spectrum decays slowly. To address this challenge, we propose UnifaSVD, a unified and adaptive framework for high-performance and numerically reliable SVD on GPUs. UnifaSVD combines a numerically stable Householder QB (HQB) factorization for numerical rank estimation with a unified EVD-based SVD backend for efficient computation of the required singular values and vectors. Its adaptive architecture supports full-rank, low-rank, and unknown-rank matrices by dynamically selecting an appropriate computational path according to matrix characteristics and user-specified numerical requirements. Rather than relying on a fixed decomposition strategy, UnifaSVD integrates efficient factorization, adaptive rank handling, and lightweight refinement within a single framework. Experimental results show that UnifaSVD achieves numerical accuracy close to full SVD while delivering substantially higher performance across a wide range of tested cases. By automating algorithm selection based on matrix properties and numerical requirements, UnifaSVD provides a robust and efficient solution for SVD on modern GPU architectures.

abstract: Deep learning (DL) compilers rely on cost models and auto-tuning to optimize tensor programs for target hardware. However, existing approaches depend on large offline datasets, incurring high collection costs and offering suboptimal transferability across platforms. In this paper, we introduce TCL , a novel efficient and transferable compiler framework for fast tensor program optimization across diverse hardware platforms to address these challenges. Specifically, TCL is built on three core enablers: (1) the RDU Sampler , a data-efficient active learning strategy that selects only 10% of tensor programs by jointly optimizing R epresentativeness, D iversity, and U ncertainty, substantially reducing data collection costs while maintaining near-original model accuracy; (2) a new Mamba-based cost model that efficiently captures long-range schedule dependencies while achieving a favorable trade-off between prediction accuracy and computational cost through reduced parameterization and lightweight sequence modeling; and (3) a continuous knowledge distillation framework that effectively and progressively transfers knowledge across multiple hardware platforms while avoiding the parameter explosion and data dependency issues typically caused by traditional multi-task learning. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of each individual enabler and the holistic TCL framework. When optimizing a range of mainstream DL models on both CPU and GPU platforms, TCL achieves, on average, 16.8 × and 12.48 × faster tuning time, and 1.20 × and 1.13 × lower inference latency, respectively, compared to Tenset-MLP.

abstract: With the stagnation of single-threaded performance, the need for optimizations targeting sequential code performance is greater than ever before. Modern workloads have also been growing in code footprint, exposing a bottleneck in the processor front-end, specifically its inability to maintain a sufficiently high fetch throughput to saturate available execution units. To address them, two optimizations exist in modern processors: (1) Fetch-Directed Instruction Prefetching (FDIP) and (2) the micro-op cache ( μ op cache), both of which improve fetch throughput leading to improved overall performance. However, since they target the same code regions, in the presence of FDIP, the μ op cache becomes mostly redundant as a performance optimization. This work proposes JumpStart : a novel and lightweight mechanism that synergistically exploits hints from FDIP to early-detect a μ op cache miss and wake up the decode pipeline ahead of time, alleviating a key front-end bottleneck.

abstract: Spatial accelerators can significantly enhance the computational performance of deep neural networks (DNNs) by mapping each layer across spatial and temporal dimensions. However, state-of-the-art mapping tools predominantly rely on perfect factorization mapping (PFM), which restricts tile sizes to exact divisors of tensor dimensions and may overlook high-quality mappings in the broader design space. To address this limitation, we propose MARS, the first efficient exploration framework designed for Ruby space. Ruby space is defined as a generalized mapping space that relaxes the factor-only constraint by allowing any integer tile size within the valid range of a dimension. MARS first models the coupling of partitioning, scheduling, and hardware resource constraints in Ruby space as a constrained optimization problem. It then relaxes the discrete mapping space into a continuous domain and employs a combination of linear programming and a genetic algorithm to rapidly obtain high-quality candidate mappings. Experimental results on representative DNN models show that MARS achieves a reduction of \(15\% \) to \(65\% \) in energy-delay product compared to state-of-the-art methods on average. Furthermore, MARS demonstrates superior exploration efficiency and consistently better mapping quality.
